Identify the lobes and ligaments of the liver, their anatomical relations, the peritoneal reflections and movements during respiration
los.html:
Position
  • Right upper quadrant under the diaphragm, mostly behind the ribs (5th intercostal space to the costal margin)
  • Moves down with inspiration (palpate the edge as the patient breathes in).
Anatomical lobes
  • Right (largest) and left, divided by the falciform ligament in front
  • The caudate (behind, next to the IVC) and quadrate (below, next to the gallbladder) lobes belong functionally to the left.
Ligament / reflectionDetail
Falciform ligamentAnterior abdominal wall → liver; free edge carries the ligamentum teres (umbilical vein remnant)
Coronary ligaments (anterior and posterior layers)Reflect from the diaphragm, enclosing the bare area (no peritoneum)
Left and right triangular ligamentsEnds of the coronary ligament
Lesser omentumHepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments (free edge holds the portal triad)
Ligamentum venosumDuctus venosus remnant, in a fissure on the visceral surface
RelationStructures
Diaphragmatic surfaceDiaphragm, (pleura and lungs above it), anterior abdominal wall
Visceral surfaceStomach, duodenum, gallbladder, right colic flexure, right kidney and suprarenal (hepatorenal pouch: Morison's pouch)
BehindIVC (in a groove on the bare area), oesophagus

los.text: Identify at the porta hepatis (the hilum of the liver): the hepatic artery, the hepatic portal vein, and the hepatic ducts.
los.html:
• Porta hepatis: transverse fissure on the visceral surface between the caudate (behind) and quadrate (in front) lobes.
StructurePosition (front → back)
Common hepatic duct (right and left hepatic ducts)Front
Hepatic artery proper (right and left branches)Middle
Hepatic portal vein (right and left branches)Back
Also
  • Hepatic nerve plexus and lymph nodes.
  • The hepatic veins do not leave here: they drain straight into the IVC on the back of the liver.
Pringle manoeuvreClamp the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of the lesser omentum) to stop inflow during liver bleeding.

los.text: Summarise the functional anatomy of the portal vein, the portal venous system and portalsystemic anastomoses and their significance in portal hypertension.
los.html:
Portal vein
  • Formed behind the neck of the pancreas (L1) by the superior mesenteric vein + splenic vein (IMV usually joins the splenic)
  • → up behind the 1st part of duodenum
  • → in the free edge of the lesser omentum
  • → porta hepatis.
  • Carries ~75% of liver blood flow (nutrients, toxins, drugs: first-pass metabolism).
Portal hypertension(usually cirrhosis)Blood diverts through portosystemic anastomoses:
SitePortal sideSystemic sideResult
Lower oesophagusLeft gastric veinOesophageal veins → azygosOesophageal varices (life-threatening bleeding)
Anorectal junctionSuperior rectal veinMiddle and inferior rectal veinsRectal varices
UmbilicusParaumbilical veins (along ligamentum teres)Superficial epigastric veinsCaput medusae
RetroperitoneumColic veinsLumbar, renal veinsRetroperitoneal varices
Bare area of liverLiver veinsPhrenic veins
  • Other effects: splenomegaly (hypersplenism → low platelets), ascites. TIPS (shunt from portal to hepatic vein) reduces the pressure.

los.text: Identify the position (in relation to the ribs) and form of the spleen in relation to its palpation through the abdominal wall and its key anatomical relationships with other abdominal structures.
los.html:
Position
  • Left hypochondrium, under ribs 9–11, its long axis along the 10th rib
  • Does not usually reach in front of the midaxillary line
  • ~12 × 7 × 3 cm ("1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11": 1 × 3 × 5 inches, 7 oz, ribs 9–11).
FormDiaphragmatic (convex) and visceral surfaces; notched superior border (felt when enlarged); hilum.
Palpation
  • Normal spleen is not palpable
  • It must enlarge about 3 times to be felt.
  • It enlarges down and towards the right iliac fossa
  • You can't get above it
  • It has a notch
  • Moves with breathing
  • and is dull to percussion (unlike a kidney, which is ballotable and has a band of resonance over it).
RelationStructure
BehindDiaphragm, ribs 9–11 (and pleura and lung base above)
Front (visceral surface)Stomach
BelowSplenic (left colic) flexure
MediallyLeft kidney, tail of pancreas

los.text: Explain the significance of the anatomical relationships of the spleen in relation to trauma, chronic infections and disorders of the haematopoietic system.
los.html:
SituationWhy the anatomy matters
Trauma
  • Thin capsule
  • Very vascular
  • Under ribs 9–11: fractured left lower ribs can lacerate it → haemorrhage
  • Shock
  • Left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) from blood irritating the diaphragm
Enlargement (chronic infection: malaria, EBV, endocarditis; haematological: CML, myelofibrosis, lymphoma, haemolytic anaemias; portal hypertension)
  • Enlarged spleen leaves the protection of the ribs → easier to rupture (contact sports avoided in glandular fever)
  • Hypersplenism traps cells
Splenectomy
  • Risk to the tail of pancreas (in the splenorenal ligament) → pancreatic fistula
  • and to the stomach (short gastric vessels)
  • Afterwards lifelong risk of encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib): vaccinate and give antibiotics
HaematopoiesisThe spleen makes blood cells in the fetus and can do so again in marrow failure (extramedullary haematopoiesis)
  • Accessory spleens (splenunculi, ~10%): near the hilum; can cause relapse after splenectomy for ITP.

los.text: Identify the splenic artery and vein.
los.html:
Splenic artery
  • Largest branch of the coeliac trunk
  • → runs to the left, tortuous, along the upper border of the pancreas
  • → through the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament
  • → splits into ~5 branches at the hilum (segmental end arteries → splenic infarcts).
Branches on the wayPancreatic branches, short gastric arteries (fundus) and left gastroepiploic artery (greater curvature), via the gastrosplenic ligament.
Splenic veinFrom the hilum runs behind the pancreas (below the artery), receives the inferior mesenteric vein, joins the SMV behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
Clinical
  • Splenic artery aneurysm (rupture in pregnancy)
  • Splenic vein thrombosis (pancreatitis) → gastric varices
  • Posterior duodenal ulcers can erode the gastroduodenal artery (not splenic).

los.text: Identify the peritoneum surrounding the spleen and the two ligaments it forms (lienorenal and gastrosplenic).
los.html:
• Peritoneum: the spleen is intraperitoneal, covered by peritoneum except at the hilum; it lies in the dorsal mesogastrium.
LigamentJoinsContains
Gastrosplenic ligamentGreater curvature of stomach → hilumShort gastric vessels, left gastroepiploic vessels
Lienorenal (splenorenal) ligamentLeft kidney → hilumSplenic artery and vein, tail of pancreas
  • Both form the boundaries of the lesser sac on the left.
  • Clinical: dividing the splenorenal ligament mobilises the spleen at splenectomy; the phrenicocolic ligament supports its lower pole.

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the attachments, openings and relationships of the diaphragm, the surface anatomy and the movements it makes during breathing.
los.html:
• Attachments: sternal part (xiphoid), costal part (lower 6 costal cartilages and ribs), lumbar part (right crus L1–3, left crus L1–2; medial and lateral arcuate ligaments over psoas and quadratus lumborum; median arcuate ligament over the aorta) → all insert into the central tendon.
OpeningLevelTransmits
CavalT8 (central tendon)IVC, right phrenic nerve branches
OesophagealT10 (right crus muscle)Oesophagus, vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of left gastric vessels
AorticT12 (behind the median arcuate ligament)Aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein
"I 8 10 Eggs At 12"IVC 8, (o)Esophagus 10, Aorta 12.
Surface anatomy
  • Domes reach the 5th rib (right) and 5th intercostal space (left) in expiration
  • The central tendon at the xiphisternal joint (T9).
Breathing
  • Contraction flattens the domes (descends ~1.5 cm in quiet breathing, up to ~10 cm in deep) → chest volume increases, abdominal pressure rises
  • The crura also act as a sphincter at the oesophageal opening (reflux, hiatus hernia).
RelationsAbove: pleura, lungs, heart (pericardium fused to the central tendon); below: liver, stomach, spleen, kidneys and suprarenals.

los.text: Identify the structures that pass through the diaphragm.
los.html:
StructureThrough
IVCCaval opening (T8)
Right phrenic nerveCaval opening
Oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of left gastric artery and veinOesophageal hiatus (T10)
Aorta, thoracic duct, azygos (and hemiazygos) veinAortic hiatus (T12, behind the diaphragm)
Left phrenic nervePierces the left dome
Greater, lesser and least splanchnic nervesPierce the crura
Sympathetic trunksBehind the medial arcuate ligaments
Superior epigastric vesselsSternocostal triangle (foramen of Morgagni)
Subcostal nerve and vesselsBehind the lateral arcuate ligament
  • Hernias: hiatus hernia (sliding or rolling, at the oesophageal hiatus); congenital Bochdalek (posterolateral, left) and Morgagni (anterior) hernias.

los.text: Explain referred pain from the diaphragm and its underlying peritoneum.
los.html:
Source of irritationNervePain felt
Central diaphragm and its peritoneum/pleuraPhrenic nerve (C3–5)Shoulder tip (C4 dermatome, via the supraclavicular nerves)
Peripheral diaphragm (costal margin)Lower intercostal nerves (T6–11)Lower chest wall and abdomen over the costal margin
Clinical exampleWhy the shoulder hurts
Ruptured spleen (Kehr's sign, left)Blood under the left diaphragm
Cholecystitis, liver abscessRight shoulder tip
Subphrenic abscess, perforated ulcer (air under diaphragm)Shoulder tip, worse breathing in
Ectopic pregnancy rupture, laparoscopy (CO₂)Blood or gas under the diaphragm

los.text: Identify and describe the locations of the 8 segments of the liver.
los.html:
• Couinaud segments: 8 functional segments, each with its own portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch and bile duct in the centre, and hepatic veins between them.
    • Each can be resected on its own.
SegmentLocation
ICaudate lobe (drains straight into the IVC; spared in Budd–Chiari)
II, IIILeft lateral (II above, III below)
IV (IVa above, IVb below)Left medial (includes the quadrate lobe)
V, VIIIRight anterior (V below, VIII above)
VI, VIIRight posterior (VI below, VII above)
NumberingClockwise from segment I, as if looking at the front of the liver (II–VIII round the clock).
Dividing planes
  • The middle hepatic vein (Cantlie's line: gallbladder fossa to IVC) separates the functional right and left livers
  • The right and left hepatic veins divide the sectors
  • The portal vein branches divide upper from lower.
ClinicalSurgeons remove segments or hemi-livers (hepatectomy) for tumours or live donation; imaging reports lesions by segment.
